summary: Sirach 5 warns the student not to trust wealth, personal strength, delayed accountability, or presumed mercy as excuses for wrongdoing. The chapter then turns to speech: avoid double talk, be steady in understanding, listen quickly, answer patiently, and know when to be silent.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach’s wisdom as practical formation: money, repentance, and ordinary speech are treated as places where reverence for God is tested. It also continues the book’s concern that wise life requires restraint before crisis arrives.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew work into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora through the grandson’s translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, and Jewish life taking place inside a Greek-speaking Mediterranean world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction: compact poetic teaching and maxims aimed at forming conduct in ordinary life.

outline.heading: Do Not Trust Possessions Or Autonomy
outline.note: The chapter opens by warning against confidence in goods, self-directed desire, personal strength, and the claim that no one will have dominion.

outline.heading: Do Not Delay Turning Back
outline.note: The student is warned not to interpret delayed consequences as safety, not to presume on atonement, and not to postpone turning to the Lord.

outline.heading: Do Not Build On Unrighteous Gain
outline.note: Unrighteous gains are presented as useless when calamity comes.

outline.heading: Do Not Be Double-Tongued
outline.note: The unstable person follows every wind and path, while the wise student is told to be steadfast and consistent in speech.

outline.heading: Listen, Answer, Or Keep Silent
outline.note: The chapter advises quick listening, patient answering, and silence when understanding is lacking.

outline.heading: The Tongue Can Bring Downfall
outline.note: Talk can bring glory or dishonor; whispering, lying in wait with the tongue, double speech, and ignorance are rejected.

keyVerses.text: Don’t set your heart upon your goods. Don’t say, “They are sufficient for me.”
keyVerses.why: This opening sentence names the first danger: letting possessions create a false sense of security.

keyVerses.text: Don’t wait to turn to the Lord. Don’t put off from day to day; for suddenly the wrath of the Lord will come on you, and you will perish in the time of vengeance.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the warning about delayed repentance into the chapter’s sharpest statement.

keyVerses.text: Be steadfast in your understanding. Let your speech be consistent.
keyVerses.why: This positive command stands between warnings about instability and warnings about harmful talk.

keyVerses.text: If you have understanding, answer your neighbor; but if not, put your hand over your mouth.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the chapter’s practical rule for speech: answer when you can do so with understanding, and otherwise keep silent.

themes: the danger of a double tongue

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by setting your heart on goods?
questions.answer: The warning is against treating possessions as sufficient security. Verse 1 does not say goods themselves are evil; it challenges the attitude that says, “They are sufficient for me.” Verse 8 adds a related warning about “unrighteous gains,” especially when calamity comes.

questions.question: Why does the chapter warn against following your own mind and strength?
questions.answer: Verse 2 describes a person guided by personal desire and self-confidence. Verse 3 shows the danger in the form of a question: “Who will have dominion over me?” The chapter answers that unchecked autonomy is not outside accountability to the Lord.

questions.question: Is verse 4 saying that God’s patience can be misunderstood?
questions.answer: Yes. The imagined speaker says, “I sinned, and what happened to me?” because no immediate consequence has appeared. The verse answers that “the Lord is patient,” so delay should not be read as proof that sin is harmless.

questions.question: What is the danger in being “so confident of atonement”?
questions.answer: Verse 5 warns against using the hope of atonement as permission to keep adding sin. Verse 6 makes the same point with divine compassion: the chapter affirms compassion, but refuses to let it become a reason to presume that wrongdoing has no weight.

questions.question: What does “Don’t wait to turn to the Lord” ask the reader to do?
questions.answer: The verse calls for prompt turning rather than delay “from day to day.” The reason given is not a schedule the reader can calculate, but suddenness: calamity and vengeance may arrive without warning. The chapter urges action before crisis, not confidence that there will always be more time.

questions.question: What is a “double tongue”?
questions.answer: In this chapter, the phrase describes inconsistent or deceptive speech. Verse 9 connects it with being blown by “every wind” and walking “in every path,” while verse 14 connects it with shame and condemnation. The opposite is verse 10: steadfast understanding and consistent speech.

questions.question: Why does the chapter value quick hearing but patient answering?
questions.answer: Verse 11 places listening before response: “Be swift to hear and answer with patience.” Verse 12 then limits speech to situations where the speaker has understanding. The point is not silence at all times, but speech governed by knowledge and restraint.

questions.question: How can talk bring both glory and dishonor?
questions.answer: Verse 13 states the contrast directly: “Glory and dishonor is in talk.” Speech can honor a person when it is steady, patient, and informed, as verses 10-12 describe. It can also become downfall when the tongue is used for deception, whispering, or ambush, as verses 13-14 warn.

questions.question: Does the chapter treat ignorance as only a small problem?
questions.answer: No. The final verse says, “Don’t be ignorant in a great or small matter.” In the flow of the chapter, ignorance is not merely lack of information; it is dangerous because speech and action without understanding can harm both the speaker and the neighbor.

glossary.def: In this chapter, atonement is something a person might become wrongly confident about while continuing to sin; the warning is against presuming on it.
The Lord’s compassion is described as great, but the chapter says it should not be used as an excuse to continue in “the multitude of my sins.”
A phrase in verses 9 and 14 for unstable, inconsistent, or deceptive speech.
A person associated here with harmful secretive speech; the chapter says not to be called one.
